questions.question_text: Which of the following options correctly describes the cost treatment of a by-product that does not have any realizable value?

options.A: Treated as a separate product and valued at the cost of production
options.B: Allocated to the cost of main product
options.C: Excluded from the cost of production and shown as a separate expense in the income statement
options.D: Written off as a loss in the current period

questions.hint: When a by-product has no realizable value, its cost cannot be independently measured and is therefore absorbed by the main product.

questions.question_text: Subsidy provided for working capital requirements by the government will be considered as?
questions.hint: A subsidy linked to working capital (a recurring operational need) is treated as a revenue receipt, not a capital receipt.

questions.question_text: Which of the following assets is a non-depreciable asset?
questions.hint: Land has an indefinite useful life and is not subject to depreciation. Buildings, furniture, patents (amortisation), and vehicles are all depreciated/amortised.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements shows the financial position of an organisation at a specific point in time?
questions.hint: The Balance Sheet is a "snapshot" of assets, liabilities, and equity at a specific date, unlike the Income Statement which covers a period.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the main objective of financial management?
questions.hint: Wealth maximisation (maximising the market value of equity) is the universally accepted primary goal of financial management, superior to profit maximisation.

questions.question_text: How is the working capital of an entity computed?

options.A: Excess of current liabilities over current assets
options.B: Excess of total assets over outside liabilities
options.C: Excess of current assets over current liabilities

questions.hint: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities. A positive figure indicates net current assets.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum paid-up capital required to be held by the Government of India to make such company a government company?
questions.hint: Under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act 2013, a Government Company is one in which not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital is held by the Central/State Government.

questions.question_text: Which variable is compared to working capital when calculating the working capital turnover ratio?
questions.hint: Working Capital Turnover Ratio = Net Sales ÷ Average Working Capital. It measures how efficiently working capital generates revenue.

questions.question_text: In case of large fluctuations in purchase price of inventory, which method for calculation of cost of inventory should be used?
questions.hint: The weighted average method smooths out price fluctuations by averaging costs across all units, making it ideal when prices are volatile.

questions.question_text: What does the ratio obtained by dividing a company's net income by its number of shares outstanding signify?

options.B: The number of shares available for trading
options.C: The earnings per share of the company
options.D: The book value per share of the company
options.E: The dividend yield of the company

questions.hint: EPS = Net Income ÷ Number of Outstanding Shares. It indicates profitability on a per-share basis.

questions.question_text: As per which accounting concept should an asset be valued at 'Lower of Net Realizable Value' or 'Fair Value'?
questions.hint: The Prudence (Conservatism) concept requires that assets should not be overstated; hence, they are recorded at the lower of cost or net realizable value.

questions.question_text: What is the appropriate accounting treatment for general donations and legacies received by a non-profit organization in India?
questions.hint: General donations and legacies are capital in nature for NPOs and are credited to the Capital Fund, not the Income & Expenditure Account. Only specific/directed donations for a purpose are treated as revenue.

questions.question_text: What is Government of India's share in National Housing Bank (NHB)?
questions.hint: NHB is fully owned by the Government of India. RBI's stake was transferred to GoI, making it a 100% government-owned institution.

questions.question_text: In the financial statements of an entity, under which type of asset is inventory categorized?
questions.hint: Inventory is held for sale or consumption within the operating cycle (usually 12 months), classifying it as a current asset.

questions.question_text: What is the interest cost of an organisation's own funds called?
questions.hint: Notional cost (or imputed cost) refers to the cost of using one's own resources (e.g., interest on own capital) for which no actual cash payment is made.

questions.question_text: What kind of cost is opportunity cost?
questions.hint: Among the given options, opportunity cost is most closely associated with marginal cost in decision-making contexts, as it represents the value of the next-best alternative foregone at the margin.

questions.question_text: How is operating leverage calculated?
questions.hint: Operating Leverage = Contribution ÷ EBIT. It measures the proportion of fixed costs in the cost structure and the sensitivity of EBIT to sales changes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following options correctly describes the type of costing that Batch costing is?
questions.hint: Batch costing is a variant of job costing where a batch of identical units is treated as a single cost unit (a "job").

questions.question_text: A salesperson in an organisation has a fixed salary of $2,000 per month, and an additional commission of 10% on all sales made. This is an example of which type of cost?
questions.hint: A cost with both a fixed component (salary) and a variable component (commission) is semi-variable (also called mixed cost).

questions.question_text: What type of cost is advertisement expense considered as?
questions.hint: Advertisement is incurred to promote and sell products, making it a selling (and distribution) overhead.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT related to Securities?
questions.hint: The NI Act 1881 governs cheques, bills of exchange, and promissory notes — not securities. SCRA, SEBI Act, and Depositories Act all directly regulate securities markets.

questions.question_text: Which regulatory body governs Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) firms in India?

options.B: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)

questions.hint: LLPs are governed by the LLP Act 2008, administered by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) through the Registrar of Companies.

questions.question_text: Which regulator in India regulates and provides guidelines on issuance of commercial papers?
questions.hint: Commercial Papers are money market instruments regulated by RBI under its Master Directions on Commercial Papers.

questions.question_text: Which institution or entity is custodian of the country's foreign exchange reserve?
questions.hint: Under the RBI Act 1934, the Reserve Bank of India is the custodian and manager of India's foreign exchange reserves.

questions.question_text: What method is used to calculate the Sensex and Nifty indices in India?
questions.hint: Both BSE Sensex and NSE Nifty use the free-float market capitalization method, considering only shares available for public trading.

questions.question_text: As per SEBI's regulation, Mutual Funds are allowed to accept investment in cash up to INR _____ per financial year per Mutual Fund.
questions.hint: SEBI permits mutual fund investments in cash up to ₹50,000 per investor per financial year per mutual fund, subject to KYC compliance.

questions.question_text: NABARD provides refinance loans to which sector in India?
questions.hint: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) is the apex development bank focused on agriculture and rural sector financing.

questions.hint: David Malpass served as the 13th President of the World Bank Group from April 2019 to June 2023.

questions.question_text: Which of the following refers to the useful data that helps in making decisions?
questions.hint: Information is processed, organised data that is meaningful and useful for decision-making.

questions.question_text: Which of the following leadership styles emphasizes employee involvement in decision-making?
questions.hint: Participative (Democratic) leadership involves team members in the decision-making process, encouraging collaboration.

questions.question_text: Which type of planning is typically focused on the long-term objectives of an organisation?
questions.hint: Strategic planning is long-term (3–5+ years), organisation-wide planning focused on vision, mission, and competitive positioning.

questions.question_text: In which role does a manager provide vision and direction to their team, and inspire them to work towards achieving organisational goals?
questions.hint: Per Mintzberg's managerial roles, the "Leader" role involves motivating, directing, and inspiring subordinates towards organisational objectives.

questions.question_text: Which of the following types of power is used by a manager who forces employees to work and threatens them with punishment for non-compliance?
questions.hint: Coercive power is based on fear and the ability to punish. It is the opposite of reward power.

questions.question_text: What is the term used to describe the process of staffing in which the right candidate for the organisation is onboarded?
questions.hint: Selection is the process of choosing the most suitable candidate from the pool of applicants. Recruitment precedes selection; onboarding follows it.

Statements: All bread is butter. No butter is cream. All cream is bad.
Conclusions: I. All bread are bad. II. Some bad are butter.
questions.direction_text: Syllogism-based questions.
questions.hint: Bread → Butter; Butter ≠ Cream; Cream → Bad. No direct link between Bread and Bad; Butter and Bad are unrelated.

questions.question_text:
Statements: A few plants are not green. All green are colourful. No colourful is black.
Conclusions: I. No black is green. II. No plant is black.
questions.direction_text: Syllogism-based questions.
questions.hint: All green → colourful; No colourful → black. So No green is black, hence No black is green (I follows). Plants and black have no definite link (II doesn't follow).

questions.question_text:
Statements: No tiger is a dog. Some rats are tigers. All domestic are dogs.
Conclusions: I. No tiger is a rat. II. All dogs are definitely not tigers.
questions.direction_text: Syllogism-based questions.
questions.hint: "Some rats are tigers" contradicts I. No tiger is a dog → No dog is a tiger → II follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some music is videos. No book is bad. All books are music. Some bad are not videos.
Conclusions: I. All bad being a book is a possibility. II. Some music is bad. III. All videos being music is a possibility. IV. Some books are videos.
questions.direction_text: Syllogism-based questions.
questions.hint: Books → Music; Music ∩ Videos (some). All videos being music is a possibility (III). "Some books are videos" is not definite. "Some music is bad" is not definite.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some metros are trains. Some metros are lucky. All lucky is great. No human is lucky. All wise are humans.
Conclusions: I. All metros can be humans. II. Some lucky are trains. III. Some great that are lucky being wise is a possibility. IV. Some humans that are wise can be trains.
questions.direction_text: Syllogism-based questions.
questions.hint: Wise → Humans; No human is lucky. Metro ∩ Trains (some). IV is possible. I is not definite (metros could overlap humans). II not definite. III contradicts "No human is lucky."

Energy sector is dominated by traditional energy sources, comprising primarily of oil, gas and coal. These constitute about 85 per cent of India's total energy consumption, followed by renewable energy, which takes care of about 13 per cent of the pie. This trend is fast changing, as government is shifting its focus from traditional sources to cleaner and renewable sources of energy. In a bid to reduce emissions, the Supreme Court had banned the sale and registration of non BS-IV compliant vehicles with effect from 1 April 2017. The government has been encouraging development of electric vehicles (EVS) for the Indian market. This paradigm shift towards electric vehicles is going to be a game-changer for the Indian economy in general and our energy sector in particular, as it will curtail demand for oil and gas in the long run. India, being a net importer of crude oil at present, is expected to benefit immensely from the ongoing shift towards electric vehicles. Also, this shift is expected to strengthen India's fiscal position in the years to come. While companies are waiting for more clarity on the policy front, many corporates have already started investing in the development of technologies and infrastructure for electric vehicles. Several auto companies have aggressively scheduled product launches of electric vehicles over the next five years. The government has plans to make India a 100 percent electric vehicle nation by 2030 and, transport authorities across states have shown their keen interest in rolling out electric bus services. India is the world's third largest producer of electricity, with a total installed capacity of 329 GW as of 31 August 2017. Thermal energy, comprising coal, gas and diesel power, constitutes about two thirds of the total installed capacity, followed by renewable energy and nuclear power, comprising about a 31 percent and 2 percent share in the pie respectively. During the last few years, the power sector in India has been witnessing major changes, with the government promoting cleaner energy, such as wind, solar and hydropower, among others, in a bid to provide rapid electrification to the entire country. There is a sharp increase in the capacity additions in the renewable energy space. On the other hand, the fossil energy space has been witnessing a sharp slowdown in capacity additions, as is seen in the statistics of April-August 2017. Only 3,790 MW of fresh capacity was added during the period, as against a targeted addition of 14,956 mw for 2017-18. The outlook for new capacities in the thermal power space looks bleak, as there are no fresh long term power purchase agreements signed. Additionally, there is a sharp fall in the tariffs for renewable energy, competing aggressively with thermal power tariffs. To reduce its dependence on coal mining, India's largest coal mining company, Coal India, too has announced its intention to diversify into mining of other minerals such as bauxite, nickel, iron ore, etc. Tariffs for wind and solar energy, which used to be prohibitively high a few years back, are now seen competing strongly with thermal power. Solar power tariffs were R2.65-3.36 per unit last month for 500 MW capacities, as compared to the all-time low tariffs of R2.44 per unit in May 2017. Wind power tariffs have fallen to a record low of Rs 2.64 per unit in the auction conducted by SECI for 1 GW capacities. The government aims to bring power tariffs to R3 per unit, irrespective of the source in the medium term. The popularity of electric vehicles is all set to rise, with power tariffs becoming more affordable — driven by an increase in renewable power capacities. The development of improved technologies and supporting infrastructure facilities will further push demand for electric vehicles in the country. A clear shift from subsidized fuel towards low-priced clean energy is expected now, which ought to be beneficial for the country. The share of oil, gas and coal in India's energy sector is expected to fall, while the share of cleaner and renewable energy is expected to rise in the years to come.
